name: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
title: Timekeeping and Billing Narratives
answer: Timekeeping and billing narratives are the short descriptions a lawyer attaches to each time entry to explain the work performed for a client. In legal operations this record sits between internal practice management and client e-billing, and it is often the first place a bill is challenged or written down. AI support for this task means generating draft narratives from the lawyer's calendar, email, documents, and matter activity so that entries are consistent, complete, and defensible. The page covers how those drafts are produced, reviewed, and governed rather than the underlying time capture itself.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Timekeeping and billing narratives are the short descriptions a lawyer attaches to each time entry to explain the work performed for a client. In legal operations this record sits between internal practice management and client e-billing, and it is often the first place a bill is challenged or written down. AI support for this task means generating draft narratives from the lawyer's calendar, email, documents, and matter activity so that entries are consistent, complete, and defensible. The page covers how those drafts are produced, reviewed, and governed rather than the underlying time capture itself.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the systems a firm already uses for time entry, matter management, email, calendars, and document storage. A narrative tool typically connects to those sources through secure APIs or an existing legal technology platform, then passes selected activity to a language model under the firm's control. Output is written back into the time entry screen as a suggestion, not a final record. Because the source material is client confidential, the model and any processing layer must sit inside the firm's security boundary or under a contractual arrangement that forbids training on the data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core method is retrieval and summarization. The system gathers activity signals from a lawyer's day, such as meetings, sent emails, and edited documents, and maps them to the correct client and matter. It then drafts a narrative that states what was done, for whom, and why it advanced the matter, often aligning the wording with the client's billing guidelines and task codes. A lawyer reviews and edits the draft before it is posted, because the narrative is an attestation of work actually performed. Quality checks compare the draft against the underlying activity to catch overstatement or vague language.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: The main risks are accuracy, confidentiality, and billing ethics. A generated narrative can imply work that did not happen, misstate the substance of a communication, or reveal privileged detail in a way the lawyer would not have written. Firms therefore treat the draft as a starting point and keep the responsible timekeeper as the person who certifies the entry. Data used to generate narratives must be limited to the matter at hand, retained according to the firm's policy, and protected from use in training or cross-matter inference. Client billing guidelines and rules of professional conduct still control what may be charged and how it is described.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward passive and continuous time capture that drafts narratives as work happens, rather than at the end of the day or week. Tools are likely to move from simple summarization to comparing a draft against the client's outside counsel guidelines and flagging entries that will probably be rejected before they are submitted. Over time, narrative generation may become part of a broader matter intelligence layer that links time entries to budgets, task codes, and matter outcomes. The human review step will remain, but it will shift from writing from scratch to approving or correcting a well supported draft.
